name: Nutrafol
lead: Nutrafol is a branded multi-ingredient oral supplement marketed for hair thinning. Its published trials describe a proprietary Synergen Complex of standardized botanicals said to have anti-inflammatory, adaptogenic, antioxidant and dihydrotestosterone-inhibiting properties.[1]

Several small randomised and open-label studies of Nutrafol formulations in women, menopausal women, women on plant-based diets and mixed groups have reported increases in hair counts or improved self-assessment.[1][2][3][4] A 2023 JAMA Dermatology systematic review of nutritional supplements for hair loss in people without known deficiency listed Nutrafol among interventions with the highest-quality evidence of potential benefit, while cautioning that its findings should be interpreted carefully.[5]
infobox: Dietary supplement, not an approved drug
Small trials on women, menopausal women, vegan women and men

paras: Published studies describe formulations for women, women in perimenopause and menopause (Women's Balance), people following plant-based diets, and men and women of diverse ethnicities.[1][2][4][6] The trial publications state that the botanical blend targets several factors thought to contribute to hair thinning, including stress, inflammation and DHT.[1]

A 6-month randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of Nutrafol Women's Capsules in women with self-perceived thinning (26 active, 14 placebo) reported significantly more terminal and vellus hairs on phototrichogram at days 90 and 180 than placebo, improved investigator-rated hair growth and quality, and no reported adverse events.[1]

A 6-month randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study in perimenopausal, menopausal and postmenopausal women (40 active, 30 placebo) reported increases in terminal and total hair counts versus placebo, a 32.41 percent reduction in shedding by day 180, and good tolerability.[2] Further studies include a vegan-formulation study in women following plant-based diets, a single-blind six-month study in men and women of diverse ethnicities, and a multi-arm six-month study of hair fibre thickness and strength.[3][4][7]

Registered trials include studies in women with thinning hair, peri/menopausal women, and a study in men.[8][9][10][11] A 2025 network meta-analysis and other reviews have assessed dietary supplements for androgenetic alopecia more broadly.[12][13] Most Nutrafol trials are small, short and use proprietary products; the 2023 JAMA Dermatology review described the overall nutritional-supplement literature as needing cautious interpretation.[5]

Trials report no or few adverse events.[1][2] The JAMA Dermatology review found adverse effects to be rare and mild across the supplements evaluated.[5] A 2026 disproportionality analysis examined dietary supplement adverse events in the FDA CAERS database generally.[14]

card.summary: Branded botanical hair supplement with several small positive trials, mostly in women, and a cautiously rated evidence base.
card.note: Dietary supplement, not a DHT-blocking drug; trials are small and short.

quick.overview:
Nutrafol is a branded capsule of plant extracts and nutrients sold for thinning hair. Several small, mostly six-month studies in women, menopausal women and some men report more hairs per area than placebo or baseline.

A 2023 systematic review included it among supplements with the highest-quality evidence of possible benefit, with the caution that the research base is limited.
quick.mechanism: The product's papers say its Synergen Complex of standardized botanicals targets stress hormones, inflammation, oxidative stress and DHT. Those mechanisms have not been shown in large independent trials.
quick.risks: Trials report few or no adverse events, and a systematic review called supplement side effects rare and mild. It is sold as a dietary supplement, not an approved drug.
